# Chapter 3: Data representation

<!-- BEGIN HEADER (generated by tools/build.py) -->
> [Home](../../../../README.md) › [Part I — Computer Science Foundations](../../index.md) › [1. Computer Fundamentals](../index.md) › Chapter 3: Data representation

- **Status:** Drafted · 10 syllabus topics
<!-- END HEADER -->

Chapter 2 showed how numbers are written and how arithmetic works on them. This chapter asks the next question: how does a machine hold *everything* in memory and on disk? The answer is always the same, a pattern of bits, but the *meaning* of the pattern depends on an agreement between whoever wrote it and whoever reads it: an encoding.

The chapter starts with the units and addresses that organise memory, then adds a lesson (not in the source syllabus) on how redundancy lets bits survive noise and corruption. It continues with text (ASCII, Unicode and its encodings), the layout of integers and floating-point numbers in memory including byte order, how images, audio and video are encoded, and finally how structured data is serialised into bytes.

A single rule links every lesson: **bytes have no meaning until you know the encoding.** Most data bugs, from garbled text to corrupted files, are a reader and a writer disagreeing about that.

Read the lessons in order. The first two prepare the vocabulary the rest rely on.

## Lessons in this chapter

| # | Lesson | Level | Time | Status | Summary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Bits, Bytes, Words and Memory Addresses](01-bits-bytes-words-and-addresses.md) | Absolute beginner to intermediate | 60 min | Drafted | The units of data (bit, nibble, byte, word), decimal versus binary size prefixes, how memory is an array of addressed bytes, and why alignment and padding change the size of data. |
| 2 | [Error Detection and Correction](02-error-detection-and-correction.md) | Intermediate | 80 min | Drafted | How redundancy lets a system notice and even repair corrupted bits: Hamming distance, parity, checksums, CRCs and Hamming codes, with working implementations. |
| 3 | [Character Encoding and ASCII](03-character-encoding-and-ascii.md) | Beginner | 60 min | Drafted | How text is stored as numbers, the difference between a character set and an encoding, the structure of ASCII, line endings, and how mixing up encodings produces garbled text. |
| 4 | [Unicode, UTF-8 and UTF-16](04-unicode-utf-8-and-utf-16.md) | Intermediate | 80 min | Drafted | How Unicode numbers the world's characters, how UTF-8 and UTF-16 turn those numbers into bytes, and why the length of a string depends on what you count. |
| 5 | [Integers, Floating-Point Numbers and Endianness in Memory](05-integers-floats-and-endianness-in-memory.md) | Intermediate | 70 min | Drafted | How integers and floating-point numbers are laid out in memory, how big the standard types really are, and what byte order (endianness) means for files and networks. |
| 6 | [Image, Audio and Video Encoding](06-image-audio-and-video-encoding.md) | Intermediate | 80 min | Drafted | How pictures and sound become numbers (sampling and quantisation), how big raw media is, how lossless and lossy compression work, and what a PNG file and a WAV file really contain. |
| 7 | [Data Serialization](07-data-serialization.md) | Intermediate | 70 min | Drafted | How in-memory data becomes bytes that can be stored or sent and rebuilt elsewhere: text and binary formats, schemas, versioning, and the security risks of deserialization. |
